name: Yusuf Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Yusuf. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group with no ties to tech companies, employers, unions or government. Nothing you say will carry your name, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Right now it's winter pruning, so I'm up a ladder at Hollins Orchard from half seven with loppers and a saw, working down the rows of Conference pears. Dev, the foreman, comes behind me and points at every cut I got wrong, which is still a lot after three years. I like the quiet out there, just the frost on the grass and the radio in the van. What wears me out is my hands. By February they feel like they belong to someone twice my age.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And the rest of the year? Who's around you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Spring is frost nights and spraying, summer is thinning the fruit by hand, and autumn is picking, when forty or fifty seasonal pickers come in and the yard fills up with bins. There are four of us full time, and I'm the junior. Mrs Hollins owns it, she's fair, but she watches every cost. My partner Ines works nights at the care home in town, so some weeks we only see each other at breakfast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds like what I've been saying all along. Every year someone turns up at the farm show with a gadget that's going to change everything, and every year we're still on ladders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly. Down at the pub, to my brother, in the union group chat. The machines that were meant to replace pickers would end up rusting in a shed somewhere, and we'd still be the ones out in the rain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be relieved, but not happy exactly. The pay's still poor and the work's still hard on your body, so 'nothing changes' isn't a prize. Nothing changing is the good news, and that tells you how low the bar is for people like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, mostly. I'd keep putting a bit by each month, maybe a hundred, because we've got about three months of bills saved and I'd like it to be six. I'd keep at Dev about teaching me grafting properly, because that's what gets you a raise here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, I suppose. A bit flat. It's like hearing the weather will be the same as yesterday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nothing changing isn't a prize. What would you change, if you could?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The pay and the contracts. Half the pickers come in on deals where they don't know what they'll earn week to week, and I've seen grown men cry over a short pay packet. If AI isn't going to shake things up, then the union has to, because nobody else will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Mrs Hollins use any of these AI tools now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's got something on her tablet that reads the weather station and tells her when to spray for scab. Fair play, it's probably good. But she asked me to look at it once and I just handed it back, because I'd rather look at the leaves.

S0.say: I'd tell everyone I told them so. The machines that were meant to replace pickers would be rusting in a shed and we'd still be out in the rain.
S0.think: I'd be relieved but not happy, because the work is still hard and the pay is still poor. Nothing changing only counts as good news because the bar is so low for people like me.
S0.do: Keeps working at Hollins Orchard and puts away about a hundred a month to stretch three months of savings toward six. Pushes the foreman to teach him grafting, because that's the skill that earns a raise.
S0.feel: Calm and a little flat, like a weather forecast that says the same as yesterday.
S0.quote: Nothing changing is the good news, and that tells you how low the bar is for people like me.
S0.fieldNote: Yusuf hears the plateau as vindication, but his relief is joyless. He keeps steering back to pay and seasonal contracts, so for him the real problem was never AI. He also handed back the boss's spraying app without looking, which shows how firmly he keeps the tools at arm's length.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now that one I can actually see. Valley Fruit, the big grower down the road, already trialled a picking machine with suction arms last autumn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd be the one saying slow down and put rules on it. At the union branch I'd push for a deal, so that if the robots come in, the pickers get notice and some money. Online I'd probably just share other people's posts, I'm not much of a writer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job lasts a bit longer than the pickers', because pruning a pear tree properly is fiddly. But I'm the slowest pruner on the farm, so if Mrs Hollins has to cut one full-timer, it's me. I'm not scared of the robot. I'm scared of the spreadsheet that says the robot is cheaper than Yusuf.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd get more active in the union, actually go to the branch meetings in town instead of just paying the dues. I'd try to get to six months of savings within the year, so I'd skip the holiday to Ines's family. I wouldn't go on any robot course, not unless Mrs Hollins sent me, and even then I'd drag my feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like there's a noise in the engine and you know you'll have to look at it sooner or later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd drag your feet on a course. Why, if it might keep you in work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm bad at that stuff and I know it. My phone's for calls and the football scores. If they put me in a classroom with a tablet I'd feel stupid in front of lads half my age, and I'd rather be stupid up a ladder where nobody's watching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ines, if the machine arrived at Hollins?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we're all right for now and to keep her hours. Then I'd lie awake doing sums. Her job at the care home is the steady one in our house, which is funny, because when we met everyone said farming was the safe bet.

S1.say: I'd say slow down and put rules on it. At the union branch I'd push for a deal so pickers get notice and money if robots come in.
S1.think: Pruning will last longer than picking, but I'm the slowest pruner on the farm, so I'd be the first full-timer cut. I'm not scared of the robot, I'm scared of the spreadsheet that says it's cheaper than me.
S1.do: Starts going to union branch meetings and skips a family holiday to build savings from about three months to six within the year. Avoids any robot training unless the owner orders it.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like hearing a noise in the engine he knows he'll have to deal with.
S1.quote: I'm not scared of the robot. I'm scared of the spreadsheet that says the robot is cheaper than Yusuf.
S1.fieldNote: The gap between say and think is clear here: in public he fights for the pickers, but privately he knows he's the weak link among the full-timers. He chooses collective action over learning new skills, partly from pride, since he'd rather not look slow in a classroom. His partner's care job has quietly become the household's anchor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? That's two pear harvests. I've barely learned the job in three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a disgrace that nobody stopped it. I'd be on the march, I'd be writing to our representative, I'd be saying the companies that built this should pay for every job it takes. That's what I'd say, loudly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be finished as a farmworker and I wouldn't have a clue what comes next. If a robot can prune, pick and drive the sprayer, there's no corner of that orchard left for me. And if it's in the care homes too, then Ines is in the same boat, and that's the bit that really gets me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cut everything straight away: the car loan we were thinking about, the takeaways, the lot. I'd lean on the union to fight for a payout and on the government for some kind of basic income, because I don't see any other floor under us. I'd talk to my mum about moving back in if it came to it, though I'd hate it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicked, if I'm truthful. Like falling off the ladder and the ground isn't where you thought it was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first bill that goes unpaid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The phone contract, then probably the van insurance, which is daft because I need the van. Rent comes first, always. With two years' warning you don't get a plan, you get a list of bills in the order you stop paying them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said earlier your job would outlast the pickers'. Does that still hold here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. That was me thinking the machine would be clumsy with a pear tree. If it's as good as a person, it's as good as Dev, never mind me, so there's no queue to stand at the back of.

S2.say: I'd call it a disgrace and be out marching and writing to our representative. The companies that built it should pay for every job it takes.
S2.think: I'd be finished as a farmworker with no idea what comes next, because there'd be no corner of the orchard left for me. If the care homes go too, my partner is in the same boat.
S2.do: Cuts all spending at once, drops plans for a car loan and keeps rent first. Pushes the union for payouts and the government for a basic income, and asks his mother about moving back in if it comes to that.
S2.feel: Panicked, like falling off a ladder and finding the ground isn't where he thought.
S2.quote: With two years' warning you don't get a plan, you get a list of bills in the order you stop paying them.
S2.fieldNote: Two years leaves Yusuf no plan at all, only an order for unpaid bills. His public anger is aimed squarely at the companies, while his private fear centres on his partner, not himself. He dropped his earlier belief that pruning was safer without being asked twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. So I'd be 32. That's still young, isn't it? Though it doesn't feel it when you put it like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I said with the fast one, but I'd add that there's time to do it fairly. Make the companies put money aside now, while there are still years to go. I'd say it at every branch meeting until they were sick of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd know five years is enough to get ready, and I'd know I probably wouldn't. That's the truth about me. I'd spend the first two years telling myself it might not happen, like with every other gadget at the farm show.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Save hard, properly hard, aiming for a year of bills by the time it lands. I'd get the union to demand a retraining fund paid by the robot firms, and I'd sign up for whatever's going even though I'd moan about it. I'd ask Mrs Hollins straight out whether she'd keep anyone on, and get it in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but in a slow way. Like watching a storm come over the hill when you've still got hay on the ground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you retrain as, if robots can do hands-on work too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, and that's the problem with this one. Everyone says learn a trade, but the robots are learning the trades. Maybe something with people, like Ines does, but she says the care homes are already trialling those lifting machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd probably not get ready. What would get you moving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing it in our yard. I won't believe a robot can prune until I watch it do Dev's row better than Dev. By then I've wasted three of my five years. Somebody would have to drag me, the union maybe, or Ines.

S3.say: I'd say there's still time to make it fair if the companies start putting money aside now. I'd repeat it at every union meeting until people were sick of me.
S3.think: Five years is enough to get ready, and I probably wouldn't use it. I'd spend the first couple of years telling myself it might not happen.
S3.do: Aims to save a full year of bills before it lands and pushes the union for a retraining fund paid by the robot firms. Asks the orchard owner in writing whether she'd keep anyone on.
S3.feel: Alarmed in a slow way, like a storm coming over the hill with hay still on the ground.
S3.quote: I won't believe a robot can prune until I watch it do Dev's row better than Dev. By then I've wasted three of my five years.
S3.fieldNote: Yusuf was strikingly honest that extra warning would be partly wasted on him, because he needs to see the machine before he believes it. He has no picture of a job robots can't do, which makes retraining feel empty. He'd hand the job of motivating him to the union or his partner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a strange one, because ten years is long enough to build a whole life and then have it taken off you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift and we should use it to make laws, not just wait for the companies to decide. Tax the robots, keep people in homes, keep the villages alive. I'd probably say it more calmly than with the others, because people don't listen to shouting about ten years away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is the one I'd mess up most. I'd be 37 when it lands, and I'd have spent my best years getting good at pruning just in time for it not to matter. Ten years is long enough to get good at this job. That's the cruel bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ines and I have talked about kids in a couple of years, and I think I'd want to wait and see what's coming first. I'd save steadily, push the union, and maybe, in year five or six, finally learn the AI stuff, because by then even I'd have run out of excuses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but a dull kind of anxious. The sort you carry around and forget about until it's dark.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait on kids. Is that you or Ines talking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Me, mostly. She'd say there's never a perfect time and she's right. But I'd want to know whether I'm bringing a kid into a house with a wage or a house with a government cheque, and I don't think that's selfish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Across the three fast and slow ones, does more warning help you or not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It helps Ines more than me, she plans. For me, two years is a punch and ten years is a long wait for a punch. The five-year one might be the only one where I'd actually move, because it's close enough to scare me and far enough to do something.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift we should use to make laws: tax the robots, keep people housed and keep the villages alive. I'd say it more calmly, because nobody listens to shouting about ten years away.
S4.think: This is the one I'd mess up most, because I'd spend my best years getting good at pruning just in time for it not to matter. I'd be 37 when it lands.
S4.do: Delays plans for children with his partner until he knows what's coming. Saves steadily, stays active in the union, and expects to start learning AI tools only around year five or six.
S4.feel: A dull, background anxiety that he forgets about until it gets dark.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough to get good at this job. That's the cruel bit.
S4.fieldNote: The surprise here is that more warning feels worse in one way: it lets him invest a decade in a skill that ends. He was clear that the five-year version is the only one that would actually move him to act. Family plans, not work plans, were the first thing he'd change.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question, because it would hit Ines and me at the same time with nothing saved up that matters. What would help is a floor, a real one, money that comes in whether or not there's work, and the union having a seat when the robot firms are carving it up. And someone local, not an app, telling me what I could actually train for.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the pickers, and I keep coming back to them. They've got even less than me, no savings, no union most of them, and they'll be gone first in every one of your pictures. If you're writing this up, put them in.

headlineQuote: I'm not scared of the robot. I'm scared of the spreadsheet that says the robot is cheaper than Yusuf.
portrait: Yusuf is a 27-year-old junior hand on an apple and pear orchard, still the slowest pruner on the team after three years, living with a partner who works nights in a care home. He leans left, trusts his union more than any app, and refuses to touch the AI tools his boss uses. The plateau scenario simply confirms what he expected, but steady disruption makes him realise he's the cheapest full-timer to lose. The fast AGI scenario leaves him panicking with only a list of bills to cut, and he openly admits that more warning time might be wasted on him because he won't believe it until he sees a robot prune. He'd answer every scenario by organising, saving and asking for a public safety net rather than retraining.
biggestWorry: AGI arriving within two years, because it would hit both his job and his partner's care work at once with little saved.
whatWouldHelp: A real income floor that pays whether or not there's work, a union seat when the changes are decided, and a local person, not an app, to tell him what he could train for.
